sections.label: Muslim retirement planning initiatives
sections.summary: Provisions exist but may not be widely known to the Muslim community, and initiatives could include culturally relevant financial guidance, seminars and outreach, and more Sharia-compliant investment options.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Such provisions are available but may not be widely known to the Muslim community.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: There are several initiatives that may assist in strengthening retirement planning for Muslims in Singapore, including providing culturally relevant financial guidance; conducting seminars, workshops and outreach programs within the Muslim community that emphasize the importance of retirement planning; developing a wider range of Sharia-compliant investment options to meet the specific needs of Muslim retirees, including sukuk bonds or Islamic equity funds.

sections.label: Three well-being strategies
sections.summary: The three strategies are charting Singapore's well-being with a Well-being Index, doing less to achieve more, and enhancing collaboration with citizens.

sentences.speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: The three strategies are: one, charting Singapore’s well-being with a Well-being Index; two, doing less to achieve more; and three, enhancing collaboration with citizens.

sections.label: Preschool subsidies for non-working mothers
sections.summary: One measure is the extension of preschool subsidies for non-working mothers.

sentences.speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: One is the extension of preschool subsidies for non-working mothers.

sections.label: SkillsFuture Level-Up Programme training allowance
sections.summary: The other measure is the SkillsFuture Level-Up Programme, which provides a training allowance to those who embark on full-time courses.

sentences.speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: The other is the SkillsFuture Level-Up Programme – providing training allowance to those who embark on full-time courses.

sections.label: Singapore Government Partnerships Office resourcing
sections.summary: The Singapore Government Partnerships Office is a positive step forward that must be adequately resourced and developed.

sentences.speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: The Singapore Government Partnerships Office (SGPO) is hence a positive step forward that must be adequately resourced and developed.

sections.label: Training SGPO and PA facilitators
sections.summary: The speaker urges resources for SGPO and PA to train facilitators and right-size salaries to hire skilled people for early policy engagement.

sentences.speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: This is good and we can do more.

sentences.speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: I urge relevant resources for the SGPO and People’s Association (PA) to train and leapfrog facilitation capabilities to right-size salaries to make sure they are realistic and adequate to hire relevantly skilled people.

sentences.speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: Such support to public agencies is critical for meaningful inclusion to engage Singaporeans in sometimes contentious and difficult conversations and to do so in early stages of policy-making to avoid U-turns on policies and avoid unnecessary spending.

sections.label: Shifting to appreciation-based culture
sections.summary: The speaker says three years as Nee Soon South grassroots advisor showed shifting from a performance-based to an appreciation-based culture makes hard work worth it.

sentences.speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: As my past three years being grassroots advisor in Nee Soon South has shown me, when people enjoy working together, they feel cared for and appreciated, the hard work is worth it.

sentences.speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: And this, we can only achieve by shifting the balance from a performance-based culture to an appreciation-based culture.

sections.label: Citizens and Government working together
sections.summary: The speaker concludes with strategies: tracking well-being, achieving more with less, enhancing citizen collaboration, and adopting strength-based and trust-based lenses.

sentences.speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: Citizens and the Government can work together so that even with fewer people, we can still get things done and sustain physical and mental health as well as continued prosperity. : With that, I conclude with a prayer that the strategies I offer – tracking our well-being, achieving more with less, enhancing collaboration with citizens, and above all, adopting a strength-based and trust-based lens, will help us on a Uniquely Singapore holy grail, towards the biggest, hairiest and most audacious goal of them all – well-being while sustaining high-growth in our economy.

sections.label: Migrant worker dormitory space standards
sections.summary: The speaker contrasts NSFs' seven square metres with migrant workers' dormitory space, asking for increases to 3.6 square metres by 2030 and 4.2 by 2040.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: By contrast, each NSF in SAF gets seven square metres of sleeping and resting space.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: Viruses will not discriminate between our migrant workers and our NSFs.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: We are now asking for dormitories to improve this from 3.5 square metres to 3.6 square metres per migrant worker by 2030 and 4.2 squares metres by 2040.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: To put things into perspective 0.1 square metre is less than the size of two A4 pieces of paper.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: Currently there is no requirement for spacing between beds.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: It is only in 2040 that we will mandate a spacing of one metre between the beds.

sections.label: Kickback investigations and employer enforcement
sections.summary: The speaker repeats a call, noting MOM investigated 210 kickback cases per year from 2021 to 2023 and took 70 employers to task yearly.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: I have called for this in my previous Adjournment Motion and I am calling for it again.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: We know that from 2021 to 2023, MOM investigated 210 cases of kickbacks per year and took 70 employers to task each year.

sections.label: Worker fear of reporting abuse
sections.summary: The speaker says laws cannot be enforced if workers fear reporting abuse, citing migrant workers coerced into paying $3,000 in kickbacks.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: We cannot enforce our laws if workers are fearful of reporting abuses when they happen.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: I have personally spoken with migrant workers whose employers coerced them into paying a sum of $3,000 in kickbacks.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: For some, this is more than four times their monthly salary.

sections.label: Worker paying boss for permit renewal
sections.summary: A worker had to choose between paying his boss $3,000 to renew his Work Permit or being repatriated.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: The worker faced the stark choice of paying his boss $3,000 to renew his Work Permit or face repatriation.

sections.label: Kickback penalties versus corruption penalties
sections.summary: Kickback penalties are a $30,000 fine and/or two years' jail per charge, versus $100,000 and/or five years for corruption; a raise is proposed.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: The penalty for collecting kickbacks is a fine of up to $30,000 and/or imprisonment of up to two years per charge.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: By contrast, the punishment of corruption is a fine of up to $100,000 and/or imprisonment of up to five years per charge.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: We need to review the penalties for employment kickbacks to ensure that they are commensurate with the penalties for corruption.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: I propose that the maximum sentence be raised to five years of imprisonment and/or a $100,000 fine, matching the penalty for bribery under the Prevention of Corruption Act.

sections.label: Whistle-blower protection for informers
sections.summary: Witnesses cannot disclose informers' names or identifying information, and whistle-blower protection is proposed for those reporting kickbacks.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: No witness is permitted to disclose the name of informers or any information which may lead to the discovery of the informer.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: I propose that we introduce whistle-blower protection for informers who report kickbacks paid to employers.

sections.label: CPF top-up and wage gap
sections.summary: The speaker questions Mr Xie on the ITE Progression Award CPF top-up, saying recipients are diploma holders earning polytechnic graduate salaries.

sentences.speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: In my speech on Monday, I said that the $10,000 Central Provident Fund (CPF) top-up in the Institute of Technical Education (ITE) Progression Award is differentiated treatment between polytechnic graduates.

sentences.speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: In response, the hon Member Mr Xie Yao Quan yesterday made the point that it is fair and right to compensate for the wage gap between ITE graduates and polytechnic graduates.

sentences.speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: But my point is that because this CPF top-up is given to them after they have completed their diploma courses, they are not just ITE graduates, they are Diploma holders and will be earning salaries as polytechnic graduates.

sentences.speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: So, can Mr Xie clarify what wage gap he is talking about?

sentences.speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: Also, going by his logic, does Mr Xie similarly think that it is fair and right to give a CPF top-up to polytechnic graduates who progress to university, to compensate for the wage gap between polytechnic graduates and university graduates?

sections.label: Ministers' position on Xie's view
sections.summary: The speaker seeks clarification from Ministers on whether they agree with Mr Xie's position and on two earlier questions.

sentences.speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: Since Mr Xie is a People's Action Party (PAP) backbencher, I would also like to seek clarification from the Ministers whether they agree with Mr Xie's position and what is the position on my last two questions to Mr Xie?

sections.label: MAS monetary policy tightening
sections.summary: MAS tightened monetary policy five consecutive times from October 2021; without this, 2023 core inflation would have been 6.6% instead of 4.2%.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: MAS tightened monetary policy five consecutive times starting in October 2021.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: Had MAS not acted, core inflation for the whole of 2023 would have been 6.6%, instead of 4.2%.

sections.label: BTO flat prices and incomes
sections.summary: Over 10 years, the average price of a 4-room BTO flat in non-mature estates stayed relatively stable while median household incomes rose.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: Over the last 10 years, the average price of a 4-room Build-To-Order (BTO) flat in non-mature estates has remained relatively stable, even as median household incomes increased.

sections.label: Inflation pressures and Assurance Package
sections.summary: Inflation is moderating but prices remain relatively high, so the Assurance Package was enhanced in the Budget.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: This year, while inflation is moderating, we recognise that prices are still relatively high and there will be continued pressures for families and individuals.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: That is why I had enhanced the Assurance Package in the Budget.

sections.label: Assurance Package inflation coverage
sections.summary: It fully covers lower-income households' inflation spending increase this year and substantially covers middle-income households' increase.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: For lower-income households, it will fully cover their increase in spending due to inflation this year.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: For middle-income households, it will substantially cover the increase in spending due to inflation this year.

sections.label: Offsetting employer contribution increases
sections.summary: Higher business costs will result, but the Government will offset half the increase in employer contributions for 2025.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: Again, this will lead to higher costs for businesses.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: But the Government will offset half the increase in employer contributions for 2025.

sections.label: Productivity and economic growth target
sections.summary: Productivity improvements are the only way, aiming for 2% to 3% average annual economic growth over the next decade.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: The only way is through productivity improvements, something which Deputy Prime Minister Heng emphasised yesterday.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: We aim for 2% to 3% economic growth per annum over the next decade on average.

sections.label: Investment promotion and R&D spending
sections.summary: Strategies include attracting high-quality investments via the Refundable Investment Credit and topping up RIE2025 to sustain R&D at about 1% of GDP.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: One key strategy is to attract more high-quality investments into Singapore because these investments typically involve cutting-edge and innovative activities.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: That is why we need new investment promotion toolkits like the Refundable Investment Credit.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: Another strategy is to maintain consistent and steady investments in R&D.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: That is why we are making the top-up to RIE2025 in this Budget, which will sustain Government investments in R&D at about 1% of GDP.

sections.label: Firms in Singapore
sections.summary: Collectively, they make up about 60% of the firms in Singapore.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: Collectively, they make up about 60% of the firms in Singapore: six zero.

sections.label: Outward-oriented segment economy share
sections.summary: This outward-oriented segment accounts for about 75% of the economy in nominal value added.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: Given their higher productivity, this outward-oriented segment accounts for about 75% of our economy in terms of nominal value added.

sections.label: Employment Pass minimum salary
sections.summary: The minimum qualifying salary for Employment Pass applicants will be raised to keep pace with wage changes.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: To keep pace with changes in wages, we will raise the minimum qualifying salary for EP applicants.

sections.label: Workforce and economic growth
sections.summary: Workforce is expected to grow about 1% per annum, with productivity growth of 1% to 2%, achieving 2% to 3% overall growth.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: That remains the policy intent, but because local wages have gone up, we will have to adjust accordingly, and the changes will be announced by MOM at COS.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: So, when you look at all of these different factors over the coming decade, we expect our workforce to grow at about 1% per annum, in line with the needs of the economy.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: This, combined with productivity growth at about 1% to 2%, is how we can achieve 2% to 3% growth for the overall economy.

sections.label: SkillsFuture Level-Up Programme
sections.summary: The new SkillsFuture Level-Up Programme will support mid-career workers with a substantial injection of skills to improve employability.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: For mid-career workers, the new SkillsFuture Level-Up Programme will support them with a substantial injection of skills to improve their employability.

sections.label: Supporting Singaporeans overseas
sections.summary: The government is reviewing how to support Singaporeans overseas and on return, and will redouble efforts in finance and other sectors.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: The children will have to adjust to an international school, and then come back to re-adjust to the Singapore system.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: So, we are reviewing this, we are considering how we can support or provide more support for Singaporeans under these circumstances so that we can help support them when they go overseas, when they come back and put them in a better position to be considered for leadership appointments in their respective companies.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: We have been doing this systematically in Finance for some time already and we can see the results.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: We now have around 4,000 Singaporeans holding senior roles in the financial sector, up from fewer than 2,000 in 2016.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: We now have a network of Singaporean finance leaders who come together regularly, they meet up and they support one another in their leadership journeys.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: We will redouble our efforts in finance and also in other key sectors of the economy.

sections.label: Support for involuntarily unemployed workers
sections.summary: Temporary financial support and training or job matching will be provided to involuntarily unemployed lower and middle-income workers.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: This will be targeted at involuntarily unemployed workers in the lower and middle-income groups.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: We will provide them with temporary financial support and encourage these individuals to go for training if needed, or to get matched to new jobs.

sections.label: Scheme funded by taxes
sections.summary: Because the scheme would add to business costs, it is funded using taxes instead.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: It will add to the business costs which small and medium enterprises (SMEs) and lower-income workers are already concerned about.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: That is why we have decided to fund the scheme using taxes instead.

sections.label: Social spending share of Budget
sections.summary: Half of total ministry expenditure in this Budget goes to social spending.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: In this Budget, half of total ministry expenditure is committed to social spending, which is a lot.

sections.label: Real income growth by group
sections.summary: Real incomes of the bottom 20% rose slightly faster than the middle income and twice as fast as the top 20%.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: Real incomes of the bottom 20% increased slightly faster than the middle income, and twice as fast as the top 20%.

sections.label: Progressive wages and jobseeker support
sections.summary: Singapore has progressive wages instead of a minimum wage and soon support for jobseekers instead of unemployment insurance.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: That is how we have innovated massively on the social front as we have on the economic and financial fronts.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: We have progressive wages instead of minimum wage.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: And soon, support for jobseekers instead of unemployment insurance.

sections.label: PISA results and education expenditure
sections.summary: Students do well in PISA tests of applying learning to unfamiliar settings, while education expenditure is about 2% of GDP.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: These results give us confidence – because PISA does not test rote learning.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: They test students' ability to apply what they have learnt to unfamiliar settings and real-world contexts and our students do well in these tests – and we have achieved all this while keeping education expenditure at about 2% of GDP, which is less than half the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) average of about 5% of GDP.

sections.label: Household benefits versus taxes
sections.summary: The lowest 20% of households receive about $4 in benefits per dollar of tax paid, middle 20% about $2, and top 20% about 30 cents.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: The lowest 20% of households receive about $4 for every dollar of tax paid – $4 in benefits for every dollar of tax paid; middle 20% of households receive about $2 for every dollar of taxes; and the top 20% of households receives about 30 cents for every dollar they pay in taxes.

sections.label: OECD Corporate Income Tax revenue estimates
sections.summary: OECD estimates imply investment hubs could gain 17% to 38% in Corporate Income Tax revenue, or $5 to $11 billion yearly for Singapore.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: The OECD's estimates imply that investment hubs could see a Corporate Income Tax revenue gain ranging from about 17% to 38%.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: This translates to a revenue gain of $5 to $11 billion per year for Singapore.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: Possibly for this reason, Hong Kong and Switzerland, which are also investment hubs, have estimated their revenue gains at $1.7 billion to $2.4 billion respectively; much lower than what the OECD has put out.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: So, these data points are suggestive of what the range for Singapore could be, anywhere from around $2 billion to $11 billion.

sections.label: Refundable Investment Credit in Budget
sections.summary: The Refundable Investment Credit was introduced in the Budget to update the investment promotion toolkit and support new investments, research and innovation.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: We are not in the same league, but we have to play a smart game so as not to lose ground and to anchor important investments here.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: That is why we have introduced the Refundable Investment Credit in the Budget to update our investment promotion toolkit and committed to spending more to support new investments, research and innovation activities.

sections.label: Pillar Two net revenues expectation
sections.summary: After accounting for additional expenditures, the Pillar Two move is not expected to generate significant additional net revenues on a sustained basis.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: So let us not be so naïve to think that the putative gains from BEPS will simply materialise in our favour.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: This is why, as I said in my Budget Statement, after taking into account the additional expenditures that we are likely to have to incur, I do not expect the Pillar Two move to generate significant additional net revenues on a sustained basis.

sections.label: Medium-term fiscal outlook and funding gap
sections.summary: MOF's Occasional Paper showed a funding gap of more than 1% of GDP by FY2030, projected to be closed by tax measures from the last two Budgets.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: Last year, Ministry of Finance (MOF) published an Occasional Paper on our medium-term fiscal outlook, up to FY2030.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: We showed in the Paper that our spending needs would grow as a percentage of GDP – to support our ageing population, to expand and strengthen our social system and there would be a funding gap of more than 1% of GDP if we did nothing.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: But with the tax measures announced in the last two Budgets – including the Goods and Services Tax (GST) rate increase – we project that we would close the funding gap, provided we manage the pace of spending growth.

sections.label: End of structural fiscal surpluses
sections.summary: The days of structural fiscal surpluses in Singapore are over, while promises are still delivered on.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: We make sure we deliver on our promises.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: But let us also be clear: the days of structural fiscal surpluses in Singapore are over.

sections.label: Budget as multi-year commitment
sections.summary: The Budget is treated as a multi-year commitment, with a preliminary high-level estimate of $40 billion for upcoming Forward Singapore policy moves.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: This is also why we do not look at the Budget simply as a one-year plan, but also a multi-year commitment.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: It is in this spirit that we have provided a preliminary high-level estimate of $40 billion to resource the upcoming Forward Singapore policy moves.

sections.label: Debt servicing share of GDP
sections.summary: Many economies pay about 2% of their GDP in debt servicing for accumulated debts.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: Many economies pay about 2% of their GDP in debt servicing for debts that have been accumulated.

sections.label: Opposition challenge on reserves
sections.summary: Opposition parties are invited to make drawing more from the reserves an election issue and seek a mandate to change the Constitution.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: If the Opposition parties have a different view on this, I invite them to take up the challenge that the Prime Minister issued in this House a few weeks ago: make drawing more from the reserves an election issue.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: Let us go to the people, ask them for a mandate to change the Constitution – you can ask them to do so; compel the President to let you spend 60%, 75% or even 100% of the NIR.

sections.label: Budget and Forward Singapore agenda
sections.summary: This year's Budget is the first step in advancing the Forward Singapore agenda amid forces that threaten to pull us apart.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: There will be more forces that threaten to pull us apart.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: This year's Budget is the first step in advancing our Forward Singapore agenda.

sections.label: WP employer-employee financed scheme
sections.summary: The Workers' Party had proposed a scheme that was financed by employer and employee.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: The Workers' Party (WP) had proposed a scheme which was actually financed by employer and employee.

sections.label: WP GST stance and alternatives
sections.summary: The WP objected to GST, now accepted 7%, and advocated using reserves or increasing the NIR instead of the two-percentage-point GST increase.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: Perhaps he could also clarify: because the WP had previously objected to GST and eventually now accepted the GST at 7%, but the debate we had earlier was about the two-percentage points increase in GST, and the options, the alternatives that the WP advocated were: use the reserves, increase the NIR, do this instead of GST.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: Perhaps Mr Singh might clarify, you too, perhaps the WP would accept the 9% as a reality.

sections.label: Exchange on fiscal sustainability
sections.summary: The speaker says Mr Murali Pillai and Assoc Prof Jamus Lim exchanged views on information, policies and Budgets for sustainability, and he asked what the $40 billion committed by the Minister for Finance goes towards.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
sentences.text: I think Member Mr Murali Pillai and my colleague Assoc Prof Jamus Lim, engaged in an exchange about the information that we have to put together, policies, Budgets, to understand whether whatever we do going forward is going to be sustainable.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
sentences.text: I put the question to Mr Murali Pillay about what the $40 billion that has been committed by the Minister for Finance, is going to go towards.

sections.label: NIRC FY2023 and FY2024
sections.summary: The speaker notes NIRC for FY2023 was revised down to $22.92 billion and FY2024 NIRC is $23.5 billion, suggesting flattish growth over the two years.

sentences.speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
sentences.text: My second clarification is related to the NIRC, which the Deputy Prime Minister also mentioned.

sentences.speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
sentences.text: I do note that the NIRC for FY2023 has been revised down to $22.92 billion; and the NIRC for FY2024 is $23.5 billion.

sentences.speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
sentences.text: So, it suggests a flattish growth in our NIRC for these two years.

sections.label: NIRC share of GDP
sections.summary: The speaker says NIRC flow will not rise as a share of GDP, is stable as a share of GDP, and cannot be presumed to rise on current settings.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: And obviously, markets will move up and down then there will be impact on the net asset base.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: But what is important – rather than look at the year-to-year fluctuations – I think, is the recognition that the NIRC flow is not going to rise as a share of GDP as we have been trying to explain.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: It provides us a good stable source of revenue – it is stable as a share of GDP – we should appreciate it, but we cannot on current settings, assume or presume that this will rise as a share of GDP because it would not.

sections.label: Budget 2022 and 2023 figures
sections.summary: The speaker states Budget 2022's original estimate was negative $5.3 billion, revised to $4.2 billion, with an actual deficit of $0.4 billion, and 2023's original estimate was $3.6 billion, revised to $6.8 billion.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: One is that – first of all, the Budget for 2022 – the original estimate was a negative $5.3 billion.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: It was revised to $4.2 billion and then finally, the actual was a deficit of only $0.4 billion.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: And for 2023, the original estimate was $3.6 billion and then revised to $6.8 billion.

sections.label: Corporate income tax outstrips NIRC
sections.summary: The speaker says he had wished corporate income tax collections would outstrip NIRC within 10 years, but this year corporate income tax is budgeted at $28 billion against NIRC of $23 billion.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
sentences.text: Three weeks ago, when I spoke in Parliament, I had said that I wish that within 10 years, our corporate income tax collections will outstrip our NIRC.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
sentences.text: But within a month, I am pleasantly surprised that it has already happened because our corporate income tax collection for this year is budgeted at $28 billion; NIRC is $23 billion – 20% more.

sections.label: CPF interest rates and support
sections.summary: The speaker says Government support behind CPF allows higher rates than market risk-free rates, with additional interest up to 6% for lower balances, aiming to meet basic retirement needs, and notes complexities including the LRIS and risk in a bad year.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: The reason why we are able to provide such higher rates, compared to market risk-free rates, is because there is Government support behind the CPF system and we are providing additional interests up to 6% for those with lower balances.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: We are designing a system that will ensure that all Singaporeans who work consistently, contribute to their CPF, will be able to have their basic retirement needs met.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: There are complexities in this and it includes the LRIS that was highlighted.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: It is not so straightforward because once you introduce a new element of risk in the hope of getting better returns, you have the issue of what happens when seniors retire in a bad year.

sections.label: Budget approval and inflation sources
sections.summary: Parliament is asked to approve the Budget, with scheme details and fiscal impact to be debated later; an MAS paper attributed inflation partly to domestic drivers.

sentences.speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
sentences.text: I believe Parliament needs to know because we are being asked to approve the Budget for this year.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: We will put up, provide details of the scheme, including the detailed fiscal impact and, at that time, there will be a full debate on the parameters and the fiscal requirements and whether it is sustainable.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: In an MAS macroeconomic review paper published in October 2022, a breakdown of the sources of inflation here attributed between a third to as much as three-fifths to domestic drivers, depending on the sector.

sections.label: GST not key inflation driver
sections.summary: The situation last year is likely to continue this year, and GST is not the key driver behind the inflation spike.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: You can look at the situation last year and we are quite clear that it is very likely to continue this year as well.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: So, the impact of GST is not the key driver behind our inflation spike.

sections.label: RIC compliant with BEPS
sections.summary: On BEPS, the RIC is compliant with BEPS.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: On BEPS, the RIC is compliant with BEPS.

sections.label: Repaying Reserves after good years
sections.summary: The Deputy Prime Minister is asked whether exceptionally good years would allow putting back some Reserves drawn down during COVID-19.

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
sentences.text: Can I ask the Deputy Prime Minister, in the event of a run of exceptionally good years, better than our predictions, would there be the possibility of putting back some of what we drew down from the Reserves during COVID-19, putting some of that back if we happen to have an exceptionally good run in the future, better than expected?

sections.label: No further GST increases to 2030
sections.summary: The funding gap up to 2030 is closed, and no further GST increases are needed up to 2030.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: Yes, whether there will be a need for GST increases up to 2030.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: We have closed the funding gap up to 2030.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: The GST increase that we announced was intended for this, so we are okay up to 2030.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: We do not need further GST increases, up to 2030.

sections.label: Funding position beyond 2030
sections.summary: Beyond 2030, funding gaps and possible additional revenues or tax changes will have to be assessed, but up to 2030 the position is sound.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: And beyond that, we will have to see if, indeed, there is a funding gap, if there are increased expenditures and whether or not, additional revenues or tax changes are needed to close those funding gaps.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: But as of now, up to 2030, we are in a sound position.

sections.label: Polytechnic and ITE student comparison
sections.summary: Compares an eight-year period for a polytechnic student and an ITE student who later enrols in polytechnic.

sentences.speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
sentences.text: One student who enrols in polytechnic after secondary school, spends three years, graduates with a diploma, starts work at the average starting pay for a diploma graduate and then, works for, say, five years, so a total of eight years, as a comparison period.

sentences.speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
sentences.text: In the same eight-year period, consider another student who goes through ITE, gets a direct higher NITEC in three years, for example, and then starts work at the average starting pay for ITE graduates for two years, and then enrols in polytechnic, graduates in three years with a diploma at the end of the same eight-year period.

sections.label: Support for young ITE graduates
sections.summary: Budget policy focuses on ITE graduates before age 30 to intervene early and close gaps early.

sentences.speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
sentences.text: And so, I hope I have provided that clarification.

sentences.speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
sentences.text: I would add that the policy design that is announced in this Budget to focus on ITE graduates when they are young, before they reach 30 years old, is an extremely important feature, because it is about intervening early in our young graduates' working lives, giving them the support as early as possible, try to close the gap as early as possible.

sections.label: Reserves top-up after 2009 crisis
sections.summary: The last reserves top-up was $4 billion in 2009 after the Global Financial Crisis, enabled by fast recovery.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
sentences.text: The last time we topped up our reserves after we drew them was in 2009, $4 billion after the Global Financial Crisis, and the economy recovered very fast, and as a result, the Government was able to top it up.

sections.label: Drawdown rates of trust funds
sections.summary: Average drawdown is about 5%, but economic-purpose trust funds have drawdown rates of 20% to 30%.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
sentences.text: The average drawdown, according to what I have calculated from the financial data, is about 5%.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
sentences.text: That 5% is based on payout divided by the asset balance.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
sentences.text: However, the trust funds that are for economic purposes, like what the Deputy Prime Minister has said, like National Research Fund, GST Voucher, public transport funds – generally, these funds have got drawdown rates of between 20% and 30%.

sections.label: GST Voucher Fund
sections.summary: The GST Voucher Fund is described as a very clear-cut case.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: The GST Voucher Fund is a very clear-cut case.

sections.label: Scheme coverage for workers
sections.summary: Asks whether the scheme will cover all workers or only lower- and medium-income workers.

sentences.speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
sentences.text: Can I clarify whether this scheme will be for all workers, or would it be only limited to lower- and medium-income workers?

sections.label: Minimum income planning target
sections.summary: MP asks the Deputy Prime Minister whether the Government has a planning target for minimum income for individuals and low-income families, and whether the Progressive Wage Supplement helps workers reach it.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
sentences.text: The next question is, can I ask the Deputy Prime Minister whether the Government has a planning target for a minimum income for an individual and for a low-income family, and has the Progressive Wage Supplement help all workers and their families to attain their minimum income?

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
sentences.text: Even if you say you do not want to put up a minimum income as an official thing, that the public know, do you actually, as part of your planning, have something to reference to?

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
sentences.text: What is the minimum level of income you want Singaporeans to have in order to survive?

sections.label: Special Account interest rate difference
sections.summary: MP asks how much more the Government is paying to the Special Account because of the interest rate difference between the Special Account and Ordinary Account.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
sentences.text: The first question is, how much more the Government is currently paying to the Special Account (SAs), because of the difference in interest rates between the SA and the Ordinary Account (OA)?

sections.label: Closure of Special Account
sections.summary: The response says the matter can be addressed at the Ministry of Manpower Committee of Supply, and that the closure of the Special Account is necessary because Singaporeans have a Retirement Account after 55.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: I think these can be addressed at the Ministry of Manpower Committee of Supply (COS) later on.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: But on the closure of the SA, we have made very clear why we do think it is necessary – because after 55, Singaporeans also have a Retirement Account (RA).

sections.label: Expanding ERS and SA migration
sections.summary: The response says the Enhanced Retirement Sum will be expanded to four times the Basic Retirement Sum, allowing excess Special Account monies to move to the enlarged ERS, covering over 99% of members.

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
sentences.text: First and foremost, we are going to expand the ERS to four times of BRS.

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
sentences.text: With that, the migration and the right-siting of the SA monies in excess of whatever they have beyond their FRS today, can then go over to the enlarged ERS and that should cover more than 99% of members.

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
sentences.text: I do not think that there is any system in the world, any financial institution in the world, any banks in the world that will pay a long-term, assured interest rate and allow you the flexibility to withdraw like an ATM machine.

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
sentences.text: I think it is one of those policy moves that we are now doing to ensure that the monies that are meant for long-term savings be sited in a long-term retirement account.
